title: Pseudepigrapha in the New Testament
subtitle: Why an apostolic name is an attribution to investigate, not a conclusion
summary: Some New Testament letters claim apostolic authorship that many scholars dispute, especially 2 Peter and the Pastoral Epistles. The issue differs from an unnamed narrative: here a named claim is being tested. Historical authorship, ancient literary convention, and a church's judgment of inspiration are distinct questions, and Islam must apply comparable rigor to its own transmitted reports.

seo.metaTitle: Pseudepigrapha in the New Testament: The 2 Peter Question
seo.metaDescription: Disputed apostolic authorship, 2 Peter, conservative replies, and why reception and inspiration do not automatically settle who wrote a text.

sections.title: The Question Is Whether the Name Is True
sections.body:
Pseudepigraphy means writing under a name other than the actual author's. It differs from anonymity: an unnamed work makes no explicit named author claim to falsify.

The New Testament debate is not whether every Christian text is fabricated. It concerns particular apostolic attributions and the authority placed on them. A careful Muslim case should identify the evidence for each dispute and hear the strongest Christian reply.

sections.title: Do Not Put Every Pauline Letter in One Basket
sections.body:
Seven letters are widely accepted by modern scholars as Paul's: Romans, 1–2 Corinthians, Galatians, Philippians, 1 Thessalonians, and Philemon. Ephesians, Colossians, and 2 Thessalonians are disputed. Many critical scholars question Paul's authorship of 1–2 Timothy and Titus, while traditional defenders contest that conclusion.

Vocabulary, theology, church organization, secretaries, coauthors, and changing circumstances all enter the discussion. A majority judgment deserves attention, but it is an assessment of evidence, not permission to stop explaining it.

sections.title: Was Writing Under Another Name Harmless?
sections.body:
Some scholars propose literary conventions in which a revered teacher's voice could be represented by a follower. Others argue that false attribution was deception even by ancient standards. The intended audience and genre matter.

Second Thessalonians 2:1–2 warns about a letter supposedly from the apostolic group, and 3:17 presents a personal identifying mark. Whatever the disputed authorship of that letter, the text treats attribution as important. It is therefore unsafe to assume ancient readers never cared who actually wrote a religious message.

sections.title: A Fair Defense Must Be Considered
sections.body:
A different topic can change vocabulary, a secretary can affect style, and a surviving biography need not record every journey. These are serious replies to arguments against Paul or Peter.

They also need evidence rather than unlimited use as rescue devices. If any difference can always be assigned to an unknown secretary or lost event, authorship becomes impossible to test. The critical case is strongest where several independent features converge; the defense is strongest where it explains those features together without special pleading.

sections.title: Why 2 Peter Is a Serious Test Case
sections.body:
Second Peter 1:16 presents eyewitness testimony. Its later chapters answer concern about a delayed return and refer to Paul's letters alongside other scriptures (3:3–4; 3:15–16). Its overlap with Jude and differences from 1 Peter are also central to the debate.

The [Catholic introduction](https://bible.usccb.org/bible/2peter/0) presents the widespread critical judgment of later authorship. [Eusebius](https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/250103.htm) shows that uncertainty about this letter was not invented by modern Muslim polemic. None of the internal features alone fixes an exact date, and stylistic difference is not a mathematical proof.

sections.title: The Case for Peter and the Limits of the Debate
sections.body:
Defenders point to the explicit self-identification, possible differences of secretary and purpose, and the eventual church reception. Earlier use may also be hard to detect in the surviving record. The conservative commentary listed below develops these arguments.

Critics answer that a pseudonymous text can claim eyewitness status and that later recognition does not independently certify authorship. Thus the question remains evidential: which account better explains the internal and external record? Calling the defense impossible or calling every critic hostile avoids that comparison.

sections.title: Apply the Warning About Attribution to Muslim Sources
sections.body:
Quran 2:79 condemns falsely assigning human writing to God. It gives an Islamic reason to take authorship seriously, not a verse that names every disputed New Testament letter.

Islam also has fabricated and weak reports. Hadith criticism can reject them without treating them as Quranic verses, but the system is not proof that no fabrication survived. [Early Islamic Preservation](/articles/early-islamic-preservation) explains its strengths and limits. The same concern for date, dependence, and accurate attribution should operate on both sides.

sections.title: Can a Church Accept a Book While Authorship Is Disputed?
sections.body:
Yes. Some Christians defend the traditional author; others understand inspiration through the received text and a literary convention rather than modern authorship certainty. Those positions are not identical, and each has to explain how its authority claim handles a disputed named attribution.

Islam locates its primary scripture in a single prophetic proclamation rather than a collection of apostolic letters. That gives a different structure, not a proof by contrast. The positive case for the Quran must still establish why its claim to revelation should be trusted.

sections.title: Why It Matters Without Becoming a Shortcut
sections.body:
A disputed author does not erase every useful teaching or disprove Christianity in one step. It does challenge an argument that canonicity automatically guarantees apostolic authorship.

If your belief depends on a particular letter's apostolic status, read the competing arguments for that letter. Then compare the [Quran's positive case](/articles/why-the-quran), rather than assuming that uncertainty in one tradition proves another.

faq.question: Is an anonymous text the same as a pseudonymous text?
faq.answer: No. An anonymous work does not name its author; a pseudonymous work is attributed to someone other than its actual writer. Whether a particular attribution is false requires evidence.

faq.question: Do all scholars reject Peter's authorship of 2 Peter?
faq.answer: No. Many critical scholars do, while conservative scholars defend it. Earlier Christian reception also contained doubts. Internal and external evidence must be weighed together.

faq.question: Could a secretary explain stylistic differences?
faq.answer: Possibly. That is a serious alternative, but it does not automatically explain every historical, literary, or theological difference. It should be evaluated as part of a complete account.

faq.question: Does later canonical acceptance prove apostolic authorship?
faq.answer: Not by itself. It is evidence of reception. Christians explain its relation to authorship and inspiration in different ways.

faq.question: Does Islam have false attributions too?
faq.answer: Yes. Muslim scholars identified fabricated reports and developed criticism to assess them. The existence of a grading system is a strength, not a guarantee that every later judgment is beyond review.
